title: Role of the Nurse in Promoting Nutrition for Inpatients

headings.title: Introduction to Inpatient Nutritional Care
headings.content: Nutritional care is a fundamental pillar of holistic nursing practice in Nigerian healthcare settings. For inpatients, adequate nutrition is directly linked to faster wound healing, stronger immune function, shorter hospital stays, and reduced overall mortality. Unfortunately, many patients admitted to hospitals are either already malnourished or at high risk of developing malnutrition due to underlying disease processes, systemic inflammation, or prolonged fasting for diagnostic procedures. As a nurse, you are uniquely positioned at the frontline of patient care. You spend the most time with the patient, making you the primary observer of their eating habits, appetite fluctuations, and physical changes related to nutritional status. Promoting nutrition is not merely about serving hospital food; it encompasses identifying nutritional deficits, advocating for individual dietary needs, creating a conducive and calm environment for eating, and actively collaborating with other members of the multidisciplinary healthcare team. By recognizing that nutrition is an essential therapeutic intervention just like medication administration, you help prevent hospital-acquired malnutrition, complications, and delayed recovery. Understanding this vital role lays the groundwork for effective patient advocacy and clinical excellence throughout your nursing career in hospitals across Nigeria and beyond.

headings.title: Nutritional Screening and Assessment on Admission
headings.content: Nutritional screening and assessment are vital initial steps upon a patient's admission to a healthcare facility. Screening tools, such as the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) or the Malnutrition Screening Tool (MST), are typically utilized by nurses within the first 24 hours of admission to quickly identify patients who are malnourished or at risk. This process involves evaluating recent unintended weight loss, body mass index (BMI), and the impact of acute illness on dietary intake. If a screening tool indicates a risk, a comprehensive nutritional assessment must follow. This detailed evaluation looks at clinical history, physical examination findings for muscle wasting or edema, dietary history, and available laboratory values like serum albumin and total lymphocyte count. In many Nigerian hospitals, culturally specific dietary preferences, local food availability, and financial constraints must also be factored into the assessment. As a nurse, your accurate documentation and timely identification during screening allow for early interventions, preventing further clinical deterioration and ensuring that specialized nutritional support is initiated promptly for vulnerable patients.

headings.title: Collaborating with Dietitians and the Healthcare Team
headings.content: Promoting optimal inpatient nutrition cannot be achieved in isolation; it requires seamless collaboration between nurses, registered dietitians, physicians, pharmacists, and speech-language pathologists. Once a nurse completes a nutritional screening and identifies potential risks, a referral to a clinical dietitian is made for specialized nutritional care plans. Dietitians calculate specific macronutrient and micronutrient requirements, design therapeutic diets, and recommend specific enteral or parenteral formulas. Meanwhile, physicians authorize the dietary orders, and pharmacists manage micronutrient supplementation or total parenteral nutrition compounding. Additionally, collaborating with speech therapists is essential for patients presenting with dysphagia or swallowing difficulties following a stroke or other neurological events. In clinical practice, you act as the central coordinator who communicates changes in the patient's clinical status, appetite, or tolerance of feeds back to the multidisciplinary team. Effective communication ensures that dietary modifications are made swiftly, preventing unnecessary prolonged fasting, aspiration events, or nutrient deficiencies, ultimately championing patient safety and comprehensive interprofessional care.

headings.title: Assisting with Feeding and Mealtime Management
headings.content: Assisting with feeding and managing mealtime environments are core nursing responsibilities that directly influence an inpatient's caloric intake. Many patients experience fatigue, weakness, cognitive impairment, or physical disabilities that hinder their ability to feed themselves independently. Before meals, you must ensure the patient is properly prepared by clearing bedside clutter, offering a bedpan or urinal, ensuring hands and face are washed, and providing prescribed eyeglasses or dentures. Positioning is critically important: patients should always be seated upright at a 90-degree angle, or at least at a 45-to-60-degree semi-Fowler’s position if they are on bed rest, to prevent the dangerous complication of aspiration. During mealtime, offer a calm, respectful, and unhurried atmosphere. Feed patients at their own pace, describe the food being offered to stimulate appetite, and alternate between solids and liquids as appropriate. For patients with visual impairments, use the clock face method to describe food locations on the tray. Documenting assistance provided and observing for coughing, choking, or pocketing of food are crucial steps to ensure safe dining and adequate nutrition.

headings.title: Monitoring Dietary Intake and Hydration Status
headings.content: Monitoring dietary intake and hydration status is essential for evaluating whether an inpatient is meeting their nutritional goals. Relying solely on visual estimation of leftovers is often inaccurate, which is why structured methods such as calorie counts, percentage estimation (e.g., estimating 25%, 50%, or 75% of a meal eaten), and dedicated food diaries are employed by nursing staff. You must meticulously record what percentage of breakfast, lunch, and dinner the patient consumes, along with any external snacks or supplements provided. Simultaneously, hydration status must be vigilantly tracked through accurate fluid balance charts. Every milliliter of fluid intake—including oral drinks, intravenous fluids, and enteral flushes—must be measured against output, which includes urine, emesis, wound drainage, and stool. Furthermore, nurses should routinely assess clinical signs of dehydration or fluid overload, such as poor skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, sudden weight fluctuations, changes in vital signs, and altered mental status. Regular monitoring allows for early detection of nutritional failure or electrolyte imbalances, prompting timely adjustments to the patient's care plan before severe complications arise.

headings.title: Managing Enteral and Parenteral Nutrition Support
headings.content: When oral intake is inadequate, unsafe, or impossible, patients may require specialized artificial nutrition support, namely enteral nutrition (tube feeding) or parenteral nutrition (intravenous feeding). As a nurse, you play a critical role in the safe administration, monitoring, and maintenance of these therapies. For enteral nutrition via nasogastric, nasointestinal, gastrostomy, or jejunostomy tubes, you must verify tube placement prior to feeding or medication administration using approved methods such as pH testing of aspirates or X-ray verification. You must also routinely check gastric residual volumes, maintain head-of-bed elevation at 30 to 45 degrees to prevent aspiration, flush lines to maintain patency, and monitor for complications like diarrhea, nausea, or tube clogging. For parenteral nutrition delivered via a central venous catheter or peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC), strict aseptic technique during dressing changes and tubing replacement is mandatory to prevent central line-associated bloodstream infections. You must monitor blood glucose levels regularly because parenteral solutions have high dextrose concentrations. Managing these therapies requires vigilance, technical competence, and strict adherence to hospital protocols to ensure patient safety.

headings.title: Patient and Family Education on Nutrition
headings.content: Patient and family education is an indispensable component of promoting nutrition, particularly in preparation for discharge. Nutrition education should begin early during the hospital stay and be tailored to the patient’s diagnosis, cultural background, literacy level, and financial resources common in the Nigerian context. You must explain the rationale behind prescribed therapeutic diets—such as low-sodium diets for hypertensive patients, diabetic meal plans, or soft diets following oral surgery—in clear, jargon-free language. Involve family members or primary caregivers in the educational sessions, especially if they will be responsible for grocery shopping, meal preparation, or tube-feeding management at home. Demonstrate portion control, discuss affordable local food substitutions that meet nutritional needs, and provide written instructions outlining warning signs that require medical attention, such as persistent vomiting, unintended weight loss, or dehydration. By empowering patients and their families with practical knowledge and confidence, you promote long-term dietary compliance, prevent hospital readmissions, and support sustained health restoration in the community.

headings.title: Evaluating Outcomes and Documenting Nutritional Care
headings.content: Evaluating outcomes and meticulous documentation complete the nutritional care process, ensuring accountability and continuity of care. Throughout the inpatient stay, you must continuously evaluate the effectiveness of nutritional interventions by monitoring clinical progress indicators, such as stable or increasing body weight, improved wound healing milestones, normalized electrolyte panels, and subjective reports of increased energy from the patient. If expected outcomes are not met—such as continued weight loss or poor intake—you must reassess the care plan in collaboration with the dietitian and physician, making necessary adjustments like changing food textures, altering supplement types, or upgrading from enteral to parenteral support if indicated. Accurate documentation in the patient’s nursing notes and electronic health records is legally and clinically mandatory. Your documentation should capture baseline screening scores, daily intake percentages, fluid balance data, education provided, and the patient's tolerance to nutritional therapies. Clear, concise, and professional documentation provides an objective legal record and facilitates seamless communication across shifts and healthcare providers, ensuring the highest standard of ongoing nutritional care.
